title: Book 19 — Telemachus and Odysseus remove the armor—Odysseus interviews Penelope—Eurycleia washes his feet and recognizes the scar on his leg—Penelope tells her dream to Odysseus
paragraphs: Odysseus was left in the gallery, thinking over how, with Athena’s help, he might kill the suitors. Presently he said to Telemachus, “Telemachus, we must gather up the weapons and take them down inside. Make some excuse when the suitors ask why you’ve removed them—say you’ve taken them away from the smoke, since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship, for the sight of weapons sometimes tempts people to use them.”

Telemachus agreed with what his father had said, so he called the nurse, Eurycleia, and said, “Nurse, shut the women up in their room while I take the armor my father left behind down into the storeroom. No one looks after it now that my father’s gone, and it’s gotten all smirched with soot since I was a boy. I want to move it where the smoke can’t reach it.”

“I wish, child,” Eurycleia answered, “that you’d take charge of the whole house and look after all the property yourself. But who’s going to go with you and light the way to the storeroom? The maids would have done it, but you wouldn’t let them.”
“The stranger will light the way for me,” said Telemachus. “Anyone who eats my bread has to earn it, no matter where he comes from.”

Eurycleia did as she was told and bolted the women into their room. Then Odysseus and his son hurried to carry the helmets, shields, and spears inside, with Athena going ahead of them, holding a golden lamp that cast a soft, brilliant light. At this Telemachus said, “Father, I see a great wonder here: the walls, the rafters, the crossbeams, and the posts that hold them up are all glowing as if there were a blazing fire. There must be a god here, come down from heaven.”

“Hush,” Odysseus answered, “keep quiet and don’t ask questions—that’s simply how the gods do things. Go to bed now, and leave me here to talk with your mother and the maids. Your mother, in her grief, will ask me all kinds of questions.”

At this Telemachus went by torchlight to the other side of the inner court, to the room where he always slept. He lay there in bed until morning, while Odysseus remained in the gallery, thinking over how, with Athena’s help, he might kill the suitors.

Then Penelope came down from her room, looking like Aphrodite or Artemis, and they set a chair for her, inlaid with scrollwork of silver and ivory, near the fire in her usual place. Icmalius had made it, with a footstool built in one piece with the seat, and it was covered with a thick fleece. She sat down on it, and her maids came in from the women’s quarters to join her. They began clearing away the tables where the wicked suitors had been dining, taking off the leftover bread and the cups they had drunk from. They emptied the embers out of the braziers and piled fresh wood on them for both light and warmth, but Melantho started abusing Odysseus again, saying, “Stranger, do you mean to plague us by hanging around the house all night, spying on the women? Get out, you wretch, and eat your supper outside, or we’ll drive you out with a burning brand.”

Odysseus scowled at her and answered, “My good woman, why are you so angry with me? Is it because I’m dirty, and my clothes are in rags, and I’m forced to go begging like any ordinary tramp? I was a rich man once myself, with a fine house of my own; in those days I gave to plenty of tramps just like the one I am now, whoever they were and whatever they wanted. I had any number of servants, and everything else people have who live well and are considered wealthy, but it pleased Zeus to take it all away from me. So, woman, be careful that you too don’t lose that pride and position you flaunt above the other women here now—watch that you don’t fall out of favor with your mistress—and beware of Odysseus coming home, for there’s still a chance he may. And even if he’s dead, as you think, he has, by Apollo’s will, left a son behind him—Telemachus—who will notice anything the maids do wrong in this house, for he’s no longer a boy.”

Penelope heard what he was saying and scolded the maid. “You shameless creature,” she said, “I can see how disgracefully you’re behaving, and you’ll pay for it. You knew perfectly well—I told you myself—that I meant to see the stranger and ask him about my husband, for whose sake I’m in such constant grief.”

Then she said to her chief waiting woman, Eurynome, “Bring a seat with a fleece on it for the stranger, so he can sit while he tells his story and listens to what I have to say. I want to ask him some questions.”

Eurynome brought the seat at once and spread a fleece over it, and as soon as Odysseus had sat down, Penelope began, “Stranger, first I want to ask who you are and where you’re from. Tell me about your city and your parents.”

“Madam,” answered Odysseus, “who on the whole face of the earth would dare to find fault with you? Your fame reaches all the way to heaven; you are like some blameless king who upholds justice, ruling over a great and valiant nation, where the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees hang heavy with fruit, the ewes bear lambs, and the sea teems with fish, all because of his virtues, and his people do good deeds under him. But even so, as I sit here in your house, ask me something else, and don’t try to learn my lineage and my family, or you’ll stir up memories that will only add to my grief. I’m already weighed down with sorrow, but I shouldn’t sit here weeping and wailing in another person’s house—it isn’t right to go on grieving without end. I’ll have one of your servants, or even you yourself, complaining that my eyes are swimming with tears because I’ve had too much wine.”

Then Penelope answered, “Stranger, heaven robbed me of all my beauty, both of face and figure, on the day the Argives set sail for Troy with my dear husband among them. If he were to come back and look after my affairs, I’d be more respected and make a better showing in the world. As it is, I’m worn down with care and with all the troubles heaven has seen fit to heap on me. The chiefs from all our islands—Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus, as well as Ithaca itself—are courting me against my will and eating up my estate. So I can’t give any attention to strangers, or to suppliants, or to men who claim to be skilled craftsmen; I’m too taken up, all the time, with grief for Odysseus. They want me to marry again right away, and I have to invent one trick after another to put them off. First, heaven put it into my mind to set up a great embroidery frame in my room and start on a huge piece of fine needlework. Then I told them, ‘Sweethearts, Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again just yet—wait, for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—until I have finished a pall for the hero Laertes, ready for the time when death takes him. He is very rich, and the women of the place will talk if he is laid out without a pall.’ That’s what I told them, and they agreed. So I used to work at my great web all day long, and then at night I’d unpick the stitches again by torchlight. I kept them fooled that way for three years without their finding out, but when I was in my fourth year, as the moons waned and many days went by, those good-for-nothing hussies, my maids, gave me away to the suitors, and they broke in and caught me at it. They were furious with me, and I had to finish the work whether I wanted to or not. And now I can’t think of any further trick to get out of this marriage. My parents are pressing me hard, and my son chafes at the way the suitors are eating up his estate, for he’s old enough now to understand it all and quite able to look after his own affairs—heaven has given him a fine disposition. Still, in spite of all this, tell me who you are and where you come from—you must have had a father and mother of some kind; you can’t be the son of an oak tree or a rock.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, since you insist on asking about my family, I’ll answer, whatever it costs me: a man who has been in exile as long as I have, and suffered among as many different peoples, must expect some pain in the telling. Still, as to your question, I’ll tell you everything you ask. There’s a fine, fruitful island out in mid-ocean called Crete—thickly settled, with ninety cities on it. Its people speak many different languages, all mixed together, for there are Achaeans there, and brave Eteocretans, and Dorians in three tribes, and noble Pelasgi. There’s a great city there, Cnossus, where Minos ruled, who every nine years used to hold a conference with Zeus himself. Minos was the father of Deucalion, and I am Deucalion’s son, for Deucalion had two sons, Idomeneus and myself. Idomeneus sailed for Troy, and I, the younger, am called Aethon; my brother, though, was both the older and the braver of the two. So it was in Crete that I met Odysseus and showed him hospitality, for the winds had driven him there on his way to Troy, carrying him off course from Cape Malea to Amnisus, near the cave of Ilithuia, where the harbors are hard to enter; he could barely find shelter there from the storm that was raging. As soon as he landed he went into the town and asked for Idomeneus, claiming to be his old and valued friend, but Idomeneus had already sailed for Troy some ten or twelve days before. So I took him into my own house and showed him every kind of hospitality, for I had plenty of everything. I fed the men who were with him on barley meal from the public stores, and got contributions of wine and oxen for them so they could sacrifice as much as they liked. They stayed with me twelve days, for a gale was blowing so hard from the north that a man could hardly keep his feet on land. I suppose some unfriendly god had raised it for them, but on the thirteenth day the wind dropped, and they got away.”

Odysseus went on telling her many more convincing tales, and Penelope wept as she listened, her heart melting. Just as snow melts on the mountaintops when the winds from the southeast and west have blown warm over it and thawed it until the rivers run full to their banks, so her cheeks overflowed with tears for the husband who was, all this time, sitting right beside her. Odysseus felt for her and pitied her, but he kept his eyes as hard as horn or iron, without so much as a flicker, so cunningly did he hold back his tears. Then, when she had eased herself with weeping, she turned to him again and said, “Now, stranger, I’ll put you to the test and see whether you really did entertain my husband and his men, as you say you did. Tell me, then, how he was dressed, what kind of a man he was to look at, and the same for his companions.”

“Madam,” answered Odysseus, “it’s been so long that it’s hard for me to say. Twenty years have come and gone since he left my home and went on his way, but I’ll tell you as well as I can remember. Odysseus wore a purple woolen cloak, double lined, fastened by a gold brooch with two clasps for the pin. On the front of it was a design showing a dog holding a spotted fawn between its front paws, watching it pant as it lay on the ground. Everyone marveled at how well these figures had been worked in gold—the dog watching the fawn and strangling it, while the fawn struggled convulsively to get away. As for the shirt he wore next to his skin, it was so soft that it fit him like the skin of an onion, and it glistened in the sunlight so that all the women who saw it admired it. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—I don’t know whether Odysseus was wearing these clothes when he left home, or whether one of his companions gave them to him during the voyage, or whether some host he was staying with made him a present of them—he had many friends, and few men among the Achaeans could match him. I myself gave him a bronze sword and a beautiful double-lined purple cloak, along with a shirt that reached down to his feet, and I sent him aboard his ship with every mark of honor. He had a servant with him, a little older than himself, and I can tell you what he looked like: his shoulders were rounded, he was dark, and he had thick, curly hair. His name was Eurybates, and Odysseus treated him more familiarly than any of the others, since he was the most like-minded with him.”

Penelope was moved even more deeply as she heard the unmistakable proof he was laying before her, and when she had again found relief in tears, she said to him, “Stranger, I was already inclined to pity you, but from now on you’ll be honored and welcomed in my house. It was I who gave Odysseus the clothes you’re describing. I took them from the storeroom and folded them myself, and I gave him the gold brooch too, to wear as an ornament. Alas! I’ll never welcome him home again. It was by some cruel fate that he ever set out for that hateful city—I can’t even bring myself to say its name.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, don’t spoil your looks any further by grieving so bitterly for your loss, though I can hardly blame you for it. A woman who has loved her husband and borne him children would naturally grieve at losing him, even if he were a lesser man than Odysseus, who they say was like a god. Still, dry your tears and listen to what I can tell you. I’ll hide nothing from you, and I can say with complete honesty that I’ve recently heard Odysseus is alive and on his way home. He’s among the Thesprotians, bringing back a great deal of valuable treasure he’s begged from one place and another; but his ship and his whole crew were lost as they were leaving the Thrinacian island, for Zeus and the sun-god were angry with him because his men had slaughtered the sun-god’s cattle, and every one of them drowned. But Odysseus clung to the ship’s keel and was drifted ashore on the land of the Phaeacians, who are close kin to the immortals, and who treated him as though he were a god, giving him many gifts and wanting to see him safely escorted home. In fact Odysseus would have been here long ago, had he not thought it better to go from place to place gathering wealth first, for there’s no man living so clever as he is; there’s no one who can compare with him. Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, told me all this, and he swore to me—pouring out drink offerings in his house as he did so—that the ship was ready by the water and the crew was found who would take Odysseus to his own country. He sent me off first, since there happened to be a Thesprotian ship sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, but he showed me all the treasure Odysseus had gathered, and Odysseus had enough of it lying in King Pheidon’s house to keep his own family for ten generations. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona to learn Zeus’s mind from the tall oak tree there, to find out whether, after so long an absence, he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. So you may be sure he’s safe and will be here shortly; he’s close at hand now and can’t stay away from home much longer. Even so, I’ll confirm my words with an oath, and call Zeus, first and mightiest of all gods, to witness—and this hearth of Odysseus that I’ve now come to—that everything I’ve said will surely come to pass. Odysseus will return this very year; before this moon ends and the next begins, he’ll be here.”

“May it be even so,” answered Penelope. “If your words come true you’ll have such gifts and such goodwill from me that all who see you will congratulate you; but I know very well how it will really be. Odysseus won’t return, and you won’t get your escort out of here either, for as surely as Odysseus ever lived, there are no longer any such masters left in this house as he was, to welcome honorable strangers or help them on their way home. And now, you maids, wash his feet for him, and make him a bed on a couch with rugs and blankets, so he may be warm and quiet until morning. Then, at daybreak, wash him and anoint him again, so he may sit in the gallery and take his meals with Telemachus. It will go badly for any of these hateful men who is uncivil to him; like it or not, he’ll have nothing more to do in this house. For how, sir, are you to learn whether or not I’m superior to other women in goodness of heart and understanding, if I let you dine in my gallery squalid and poorly clad? Men live but a little while; if they are hard, and deal harshly, people wish them ill as long as they’re alive, and speak contemptuously of them once they’re dead, but the man who is righteous and deals righteously—people tell of his praise in every land, and many will call him blessed.”

Odysseus answered, “Madam, I’ve forsworn rugs and blankets ever since the day I left the snowy ranges of Crete to go aboard ship. I’ll lie as I’ve lain on many a sleepless night before this. Night after night I’ve passed in whatever rough sleeping place I could find, waiting for morning. Nor, again, do I like having my feet washed; I won’t let any of the young hussies about your house touch my feet. But if you have some old and respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I’ll let her wash them.”

To this Penelope said, “My dear sir, of all the guests who have ever come to my house, none has ever spoken in all things with such admirable propriety as you. There happens to be a most respectable old woman in the house—the very one who took my poor dear husband in her arms the night he was born, and nursed him in infancy. She’s very feeble now, but she shall wash your feet.” “Come here,” she said, “Eurycleia, and wash your master’s age-mate. I suppose Odysseus’s hands and feet are much the same now as this man’s, for trouble ages all of us dreadfully fast.”

At these words the old woman covered her face with her hands and began to weep and lament, saying, “My dear child, I don’t know what I’m to do with you. I’m certain no one was ever more god-fearing than you, and yet Zeus hates you. No one in the whole world ever burned him more thighbones, or gave him finer sacrifices, when you prayed that you might come to a green old age yourself and see your son grow up to take after you—yet see how, of all men, you are the only one he has kept from ever getting back to your own home. I’ve no doubt the women in whatever foreign palace Odysseus has come to are gibing at him just as all these sluts here have been gibing at you. I don’t wonder that you won’t let them wash you, after the way they’ve insulted you. I’ll wash your feet myself, gladly enough, since Penelope has told me to; I’ll wash them both for Penelope’s sake and for your own, for you’ve raised the most lively feelings of pity in me. And let me say this too, and pray attend to it: we’ve had all kinds of strangers in distress come here before now, but I make bold to say that no one ever yet came who was so like Odysseus in figure, voice, and feet as you are.”
“Those who have seen us both,” answered Odysseus, “have always said we were wonderfully like each other, and now you’ve noticed it too.”

Then the old woman took the cauldron she meant to wash his feet in, and poured plenty of cold water into it, adding hot until the bath was warm enough. Odysseus sat by the fire, but before long he turned away from the light, for it occurred to him that when the old woman took hold of his leg, she would recognize a certain scar it bore, and the whole truth would come out. And sure enough, as soon as she began washing her master, she at once recognized the scar as one that had been given him by a wild boar when he was hunting on Mt. Parnassus with his splendid grandfather Autolycus—who was the most accomplished thief and perjurer in the whole world—and with the sons of Autolycus. Hermes himself had given Autolycus this gift, for Autolycus used to burn the thighbones of goats and kids in offering to him, and so the god took pleasure in his company. It happened once that Autolycus had come to Ithaca and found his daughter’s child just born. As soon as he had finished supper, Eurycleia set the infant on his knees and said, “Autolycus, you must find a name for your grandson; you’ve wanted one for a long time.”

“Son-in-law and daughter,” Autolycus replied, “name the child this way: I’m highly displeased with a great many people in one place and another, both men and women, so name the child ‘Odysseus,’ or the child of anger. When he grows up and comes to visit his mother’s family on Mt. Parnassus, where my land lies, I’ll give him a present and send him on his way rejoicing.”

So Odysseus went to Parnassus to get the presents from Autolycus, who, with his sons, shook hands with him and welcomed him. His grandmother Amphithea threw her arms around him, and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes, while Autolycus told his sons to get dinner ready, and they did as he said. They brought in a five-year-old bull, flayed it, prepared it, and divided it into joints; these they then cut carefully into smaller pieces and spitted them; they roasted them thoroughly and served the portions around. So through the whole day, until the sun went down, they feasted, and every man had his full share so that all were satisfied; but when the sun set and it grew dark, they went to bed and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, the sons of Autolycus went out hunting with their hounds, and Odysseus went too. They climbed the wooded slopes of Parnassus and soon reached its breezy upland valleys; but as the sun, newly risen from the slow, still currents of Oceanus, was just beginning to strike the fields, they came to a mountain dell. The dogs went ahead, searching for the tracks of the animal they were chasing, and behind them came the sons of Autolycus, Odysseus among them, close behind the dogs with a long spear in his hand. Here, in some thick brushwood so dense that the wind and rain couldn’t get through it, nor the sun’s rays reach the ground beneath, which lay thick with fallen leaves, was the lair of a huge boar. The boar heard the noise of the men’s feet, and the hounds baying on every side as the huntsmen came up to him, so he rushed from his lair, raised the bristles on his neck, and stood at bay with fire flashing from his eyes. Odysseus was the first to raise his spear and try to drive it into the brute, but the boar was too quick for him, and charged him sideways, ripping him above the knee with a gash that tore deep though it didn’t reach the bone. As for the boar, Odysseus struck him on the right shoulder, and the point of the spear went right through him, so that he fell groaning in the dust until the life went out of him. The sons of Autolycus busied themselves with the carcass of the boar, and bound up Odysseus’s wound; then, after chanting a spell to stop the bleeding, they hurried home as fast as they could. But when Autolycus and his sons had thoroughly healed Odysseus, they gave him some splendid presents and sent him back to Ithaca on the best of terms. When he got home, his father and mother were overjoyed to see him, and asked him all about it, and how he had come by the scar; so he told them how the boar had ripped him while he was out hunting with Autolycus and his sons on Mt. Parnassus.

As soon as Eurycleia had the scarred leg in her hands and had a good hold of it, she recognized it and dropped the foot at once. The leg fell into the bath, which rang out and was overturned, so that all the water spilled onto the ground. Eurycleia’s eyes, between joy and grief, filled with tears, and for a moment she couldn’t speak; but she caught Odysseus by the beard and said, “My dear child, I’m sure you must be Odysseus himself—only I didn’t know you until I’d actually touched and handled you.”

As she spoke she looked toward Penelope, as though wanting to tell her that her dear husband was in the house, but Penelope was unable to look in that direction and see what was going on, for Athena had turned her attention elsewhere. So Odysseus caught Eurycleia by the throat with his right hand, and with his left drew her close to him, and said, “Nurse, do you want to be the ruin of me—you who nursed me at your own breast—now that after twenty years of wandering I’ve come at last to my own home again? Since heaven has let you recognize me, hold your tongue, and don’t say a word about it to anyone else in the house, for if you do, I tell you—and it shall surely happen—that if heaven grants me the lives of these suitors, I won’t spare you, though you’re my own nurse, when I’m killing the other women.”

“My child,” answered Eurycleia, “what are you talking about? You know very well that nothing can either bend or break me. I’ll hold my tongue like a stone or a piece of iron; furthermore let me say—and take my words to heart—when heaven has delivered the suitors into your hand, I’ll give you a list of the women in the house who have been ill-behaved, and of those who are guiltless.”
And Odysseus answered, “Nurse, you oughtn’t to speak that way; I’m well able to form my own opinion about every one of them; hold your tongue, and leave everything to heaven.”

At this Eurycleia left the gallery to fetch more water, for the first lot had all been spilled; and when she had washed him and anointed him with oil, Odysseus drew his seat nearer to the fire to warm himself, and hid the scar under his rags. Then Penelope began talking to him and said:

“Stranger, I’d like to speak with you briefly about another matter. It’s nearly bedtime now—for those, at least, who can sleep in spite of sorrow. As for me, heaven has given me a life of such immeasurable grief that even by day, while I’m busy with my duties and looking after the servants, I go on weeping and lamenting the whole time; then, when night comes and we all go to bed, I lie awake thinking, and my heart falls prey to the most relentless, cruel torment. As the dun nightingale, daughter of Pandareus, sings in early spring from her seat hidden deep in the leaves, and pours out, in trill after plaintive trill, the story of how by mishap she killed her own child Itylus, son of King Zethus—even so does my mind toss and turn, uncertain whether I ought to stay here with my son and guard my property, my servants, and the greatness of this house, out of regard for public opinion and the memory of my late husband, or whether it isn’t time now for me to go off with the best of these suitors who are courting me and offering me such magnificent gifts. As long as my son was still young and unable to understand, he wouldn’t hear of my leaving his father’s house, but now that he’s fully grown, he begs and urges me to do just that, furious at the way the suitors are eating up his property. Now listen to a dream I’ve had, and interpret it for me if you can. I keep twenty geese about the house, that eat mash out of a trough, and I’m very fond of them. I dreamed that a great eagle came swooping down from a mountain and drove his curved beak into the neck of each one until he’d killed them all. Then he soared off into the sky and left them lying dead about the yard; and I wept in my dream until all my maids gathered around me, so bitterly was I grieving because the eagle had killed my geese. Then he came back again, and, perching on a projecting rafter, spoke to me in a human voice and told me to stop crying. ‘Be of good courage,’ he said, ‘daughter of Icarius; this is no dream, but a vision of good omen that shall surely come to pass. The geese are the suitors, and I am no longer an eagle, but your own husband, come back to you, and I will bring these suitors to a disgraceful end.’ At this I woke, and when I looked out I saw my geese at the trough, eating their mash as usual.”

“This dream, madam,” replied Odysseus, “can admit of only one interpretation, for hasn’t Odysseus himself told you how it shall be fulfilled? The death of the suitors is foretold, and not one single one of them will escape.”

And Penelope answered, “Stranger, dreams are very strange and unpredictable things, and they don’t by any means always come true. There are two gates through which these insubstantial visions come to us; one is of horn, and the other of ivory. Those that come through the gate of ivory are empty, but those from the gate of horn mean something to the one who sees them. I don’t think, though, that my own dream came through the gate of horn, though my son and I would be most thankful if it proves to have done so. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—the coming dawn will bring in the ill-omened day that is to part me from the house of Odysseus, for I’m about to hold a contest with the axes. My husband used to set up twelve axes in the court, one behind the other, like the props a ship is built on; then he would step back from them and shoot an arrow through all twelve. I’ll make the suitors try to do the same thing, and whichever of them can string the bow most easily, and send his arrow through all twelve axes, that man I’ll follow, and leave this house of my lawful husband, so fine and so full of wealth. But even so, I have no doubt I’ll go on remembering it in my dreams.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, you needn’t put off your contest, for Odysseus will return before they can even string the bow, handle it however they will, and send their arrows through the iron.”

To this Penelope said, “As long as you sit here talking with me, sir, I have no wish at all to go to bed. Still, people can’t go without sleep forever, and heaven has appointed us dwellers on earth a proper time for everything. So I’ll go upstairs now and lie down on that couch which I’ve never stopped flooding with my tears since the day Odysseus set out for that city with the hateful name.”
She then went upstairs to her own room, not alone, but attended by her maids, and there she lamented her dear husband until Athena shed sweet sleep over her eyes.
